summary: Sets out requirements for the protocol between path computation clients and path computation elements, and for discovering them, when traffic engineering spans several network layers such as MPLS and GMPLS layers. Planning end to end across layers can make the whole network more efficient. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: In a network built from several layers, such as packet switching over optical switching, the upper layer sees the lower layer only as a map of available links. This RFC lists what a path computation element, the element that works out routes, has to be able to do so that a route can be chosen across all the layers at once.

subtitle: What a path computation element has to be able to do so a route can be chosen across several network layers at once.

tldr.problem: In a network built from several layers, the upper layer sees the lower layer only as a map of available links, so a path that crosses layers cannot be computed from one layer's view alone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC lists what the PCE Communication Protocol must carry between a path computation client and a path computation element: permission to cross layers, the type of path wanted, layer constraints, adaptation at each boundary, cooperation between elements, and diversity.
tldr.outcome: It is a requirements document, not a protocol. It supplements RFC 4657 and RFC 4674 and is meant to be used by the designers of a PCEP extension for inter-layer path computation.

sections.title: Introduction and Terminology
sections.content:
The Path Computation Element (PCE) defined in RFC 4655 is an entity that is capable of computing a network path or route based on a network graph and applying computational constraints. A network may comprise multiple layers. These layers may represent the separation of technologies, such as Packet Switch Capable, Time Division Multiplex and lambda switch capable, into GMPLS regions; the separation of data plane switching granularity levels, such as PSC-1 and PSC-2 or VC4 and VC12, into GMPLS layers; or a distinction between client and server networking roles. In such a multi-layer network, Label Switched Paths (LSPs) in lower layers are used to carry upper-layer LSPs. The network topology formed by lower-layer LSPs and advertised to the higher layer is called a Virtual Network Topology (VNT).

In layered networks under the operation of Multiprotocol Label Switching Traffic Engineering (MPLS-TE) and Generalized MPLS (GMPLS) protocols, it is important to provide mechanisms to allow global optimization of network resources. That is, to take into account all layers, rather than optimizing resource utilization at each layer independently. This allows better network efficiency and is called inter-layer traffic engineering. It includes mechanisms allowing computation of end-to-end paths across layers, and mechanisms for control and management of the VNT by setting up and releasing LSPs in the lower layers.

This document presents sets of requirements for communication between Path Computation Clients (PCCs) and PCEs using the PCE Communication Protocol (PCEP), and for PCE discovery for inter-layer traffic engineering. It supplements the generic requirements documented in RFC 4657, RFC 4674, and the framework provided in RFC 5623. The key words MUST, SHOULD and MAY are used as described in RFC 2119, for clarity of the requirement specification, even though the document is informational and not a protocol specification.
sections.plainLanguage: In a network built from several layers, such as packet switching over optical switching, the upper layer sees the lower layer only as a map of available links. This RFC lists what a path computation element, the element that works out routes, has to be able to do so that a route can be chosen across all the layers at once.

sections.title: Why Inter-Layer Path Computation Needs a PCE
sections.content:
RFC 4206 defines a way to signal an MPLS or a GMPLS LSP with an explicit route in a higher layer of a network that includes hops traversed by LSPs in lower layers of the network. The computation of end-to-end paths across layers is called inter-layer path computation. An LSR in the higher layer might not have information on the topology of lower layers, particularly in an overlay or augmented model, so it might not be able to compute an end-to-end path across layers.

PCE-based inter-layer path computation consists of relying on one or more PCEs to compute an end-to-end path across layers. This could be a single PCE path computation, where the PCE has topology information about multiple layers and can directly compute an end-to-end path across layers considering the topology of all of them. Alternatively the inter-layer path computation could be performed as a multiple PCE computation, where each member of a set of PCEs has information about the topology of one or more layers but not all layers, and they collaborate to compute an end-to-end path.

The RFC's example is a two-layer network where the higher-layer network is a packet-based IP/MPLS or GMPLS network and the lower-layer network is a GMPLS-controlled optical network. An ingress LSR in the higher-layer network tries to set up an LSP to an egress LSR also in the higher-layer network, across the lower-layer network. Suppose there is no TE link between the border LSRs, which are located on the boundary between the higher-layer and lower-layer networks, and that the ingress LSR does not have topology visibility in the lower layer. A single-layer path computation applied for the higher layer then fails. Inter-layer path computation is able to provide a route in the higher layer and a suggestion that a lower-layer LSP be set up between the border LSRs, considering both layers as TE topologies.
sections.plainLanguage: Without this, the upper layer has no path to the far side and the setup fails. With it, the computation works out both the upper-layer route and the lower-layer link that the upper layer needs, and treats them as one plan.

sections.title: PCC-PCE Communication Requirements
sections.content:
PCEP must allow requests and replies for inter-layer path computation. This requires no additional messages, but it implies the following additional constraints to be added to PCEP.

Control of inter-layer path computation. A request from a PCC to a PCE must support the inclusion of an optional indication of whether inter-layer path computation is allowed. In the absence of such an indication, the default is that inter-layer path computation is not allowed.

Control of the type of path. The PCE computes and returns a path that the PCC can use to build a higher-layer or lower-layer LSP once converted to an Explicit Route Object (ERO) for RSVP-TE signalling. There are two options: a mono-layer path, which includes only TE links from the same layer, and a multi-layer path, which includes TE links from distinct layers. A PCC may know that it is not possible, for technological or policy reasons, to signal a multi-layer path and need a mono-layer one, or it may not wish the layer border node to have control of path computation. So PCEP must allow the PCC to select the path types to be computed, and that may be returned, by choosing one or more of: a mono-layer path specified by strict hops, which may include virtual TE links; a mono-layer path that includes loose hops; and a multi-layer path that can include the path, as strict or loose hops, of one or more lower-layer LSPs not yet established. The response from a PCE to a PCC must report the type of path computed, and where a multi-layer path is returned, PCEP must support including, as part of the end-to-end path, the path of the lower-layer LSPs to be established.

If a response carries a mono-layer path specified by strict hops that includes virtual TE links or loose hops, or a multi-layer path that can include the complete path of lower-layer LSPs not yet established, then signalling the higher-layer LSP may trigger the establishment of the lower-layer LSPs. That triggered signalling may increase the higher-layer connection setup latency, so a request must allow a PCC to indicate whether triggered signalling is acceptable, and a response must allow a PCE to indicate whether the computed path requires it. A PCE may not be able to distinguish virtual TE links from regular TE links, so even when a request says triggered signalling is not acceptable, a PCE may choose virtual TE links. Because an ingress LSR of a higher-layer or lower-layer LSP may be present in multiple layers, PCEP must be able to indicate the required or provided path layer even when a mono-layer path is requested or supplied.

Constraints. A request must support constraints for a multi-layer path, including control over which network layers may, must or must not be included in the computed path, expressed in terms of the switching types of the layer networks. It may also be desirable to constrain the number of layer boundaries crossed, that is the number of adaptations performed on the end-to-end path, so PCEP should include a constraint or objective function to minimize or cap that number and a mechanism to report it when a path is supplied. The request must also allow different objective functions to be applied within different network layers: the path in a packet network may need to be optimized for least delay using the IGP metric as a measure of delay, while the path in an underlying TDM network might be optimized for fewest hops.

Adaptation capability. It must be possible for the path computation request to indicate the desired adaptation function at the end points of the lower-layer LSP being computed. This matters where the ingress and egress LSR participate in more than one layer network but may not be capable of all associated adaptations.

Cooperation between PCEs. When each layer is in scope of a different PCE which only has access to the topology information of its layer, the PCEs of each layer need to cooperate, so communication between PCEs is required. A PCE that behaves as a client is defined as a PCC. PCEP must allow requests and replies for multiple PCE inter-layer path computation.

Diverse paths. PCEP must allow the computation of diverse inter-layer paths. A request must support multiple path requests, with the desired level of diversity at each layer: link, node or Shared Risk Link Group (SRLG).

Discovery. Where several PCEs with distinct capabilities are available, a PCC has to select appropriate ones, so the PCE discovery mechanism may support disclosure of detailed PCE capabilities. A PCE may advise support for inter-layer path computation; support for mono-layer and multi-layer paths; support for inter-layer constraints; support for adaptation capability; support for inter-PCE communication; and support for inter-layer diverse path computation. PCEP should also allow the overlay, integrated and augmented models for interworking between MPLS- and GMPLS-controlled networks.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists what the request and the reply have to carry: whether a path may cross layers at all, which kinds of path the client will accept, which layers are allowed, how many layer boundaries may be crossed, what happens at each boundary, and whether two paths have to avoid each other.

sections.title: Manageability Considerations
sections.content:
Control of function and policy. An individual PCE may elect to support inter-layer computations and advertise its capabilities, and PCE implementations may provide a configuration switch to enable or disable support, with the change re-advertised. A PCE may also support inter-layer computations without advertising the fact, so that only PCCs configured to know of the PCE and its capabilities can use it. Support and advertisement of support may be subject to policy, and a PCE may hide its inter-layer capabilities from certain PCCs by not advertising them through the discovery protocol and not reporting them in any PCEP capabilities exchange. A PCE may also be directed by policy to refuse an inter-layer path computation request for any reason, including the identity of the PCC making the request.

Information and data models. PCEP extensions to support inter-layer computations must be accompanied by MIB objects for the control and monitoring of the protocol and of the PCE that performs the computations. The objects may be provided in the same MIB module as used for general PCEP control and monitoring, or in a new MIB module, and must allow the control and monitoring of all aspects of PCEP relevant to inter-layer path computation.

Liveness detection and monitoring. No changes are necessary to the liveness detection and monitoring requirements already embodied in RFC 4657. Inter-layer path computations might require extended cooperation between PCEs, however, so liveness detection and monitoring should be applied to each PCEP communication and aggregated to report the behaviour of an individual PCEP request to the originating PCC. Where a request is forwarded between multiple PCEs, neither the PCC nor the first PCE can monitor the liveness of all PCE-to-PCE connections or of the PCEs themselves, so each PCE must operate correct monitoring procedures and correlate any failures back to the PCEP requests that are outstanding.

Verifying correct operation. There are no additional requirements beyond those in RFC 4657. Verification of the correct operation of the PCE and its algorithms is out of scope for the protocol requirements, but a PCC may send the same request to more than one PCE and compare the results.

Requirements on other protocols and functional components. A PCE operates on a topology graph that may be built using information distributed by TE extensions to the routing protocol operating within the network. So that the PCE can select a suitable path for the signalling protocol to use to install the inter-layer LSP, the topology graph must include information about the inter-layer signalling and forwarding, that is adaptation, capabilities of each LSR in the network. Whatever means are used to collect the information, the graph must include the requisite information.

Impact on network operation. Using a PCE to compute inter-layer paths is not expected to have significant impact on network operations if the upper-layer traffic engineering practices are aware of the frequent changes that might occur in the VNT. Introducing inter-layer support to a PCE that already provides mono-layer path computation might change the loading on the PCE, and that might have an impact on network behaviour especially during recovery periods immediately after a network failure. On the other hand, the use of inter-layer path computation is envisioned to have significant benefits for the operation of a multi-layer network, including improving network resource usage and enabling a greater number of higher-layer LSPs to be supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything here is about running the service day to day: whether a PCE advertises what it can do, what operators can see and change through the network management objects, how failures in a chain of PCEs are traced back to the request that caused them, and what the extra load on the PCE does to the network during recovery.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Inter-layer traffic engineering with PCE may raise new security issues when PCE-to-PCE communication is used between different layer networks for inter-layer path computation. Security issues may also exist when a single PCE is granted full visibility of TE information that applies to multiple layers. The formal introduction of a VNT Manager component, as described in RFC 5623, provides the basis for the application of inter-layer security and policy. It is expected that solutions for inter-layer protocol extensions will address these issues in detail.
sections.plainLanguage: Letting several PCEs talk to each other, and letting one PCE see every layer, opens new ways in. The RFC points to the VNT Manager component as the place where the security and policy rules would live, and expects later work to fill in the detail.

viz.caption: THE PATH TYPES A CLIENT MAY SELECT

items.title: Mono-layer path, strict hops
items.text: Only TE links from the same layer. It may include virtual TE links.

items.title: Mono-layer path, loose hops
items.text: Only TE links from the same layer, with hops that the PCE may choose.

items.title: Multi-layer path
items.text: TE links from distinct layers, optionally including the path of lower-layer LSPs that are not yet established.

items.title: Triggered signalling
items.text: Signalling the higher-layer LSP may set up the lower-layer LSPs, which raises the setup latency of the higher layer.
